Operating the Machine

This page describes the complete operating procedure of the prototype, from the creation of the digital pattern to the execution of the machine.

The workflow is divided into two parts:

  1. the user computer, where the PNG pattern is created with the Pattern Editor;
  2. the machine, where the USB drive is inserted and the Raspberry Pi runs the display interface and communicates with the ESP32.

Required Software

Two different software environments are used:

Device Purpose Main script
User computer Create the PNG pattern pattern_editor.py
Raspberry Pi inside the machine Read the USB drive, manage the display and communicate with the ESP32 raspberry.py

1. Pattern Editor Setup on the User Computer

The user must run the Pattern Editor on their own computer.

The editor is used to create a PNG file compatible with the machine.

1.1 Install Python

Install Python 3 on the computer.

To check if Python is installed, open a terminal and run:

python --version

or, on some systems:

python3 --version

If Python is not installed, install it from the official Python website or through the operating system package manager.

1.2 Create a Virtual Environment

Go to the folder where the Pattern Editor script is located.

On Windows:

py -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate

On Linux or macOS:

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate

1.3 Install the Required Python Library

The Pattern Editor requires Pillow to open and save PNG images.

Install it with:

pip install pillow

If the computer uses Linux and the error No module named tkinter appears, install Tkinter with:

sudo apt install python3-tk

Tkinter is used for the graphical interface of the Pattern Editor.

1.4 Run the Pattern Editor

Run the script:

On Windows:

py pattern_editor.py

On Linux or macOS:

python3 pattern_editor.py

The Pattern Editor opens a graphical interface where the user can create, edit, import and preview the pattern before exporting it for the machine.

Two editing modes are available:

  • Single Pattern: the user draws the complete pattern directly on a 48-pixel-wide grid. The height can be selected according to the required number of rows.
  • Repeated Pattern: the user draws an 8-pixel-wide module, which is automatically repeated 6 times horizontally to obtain the required final width of 48 pixels. Vertically, the same module can be repeated several times, or different modules with different heights can be combined.

In Repeated Pattern mode, the editor displays a preview of the final 48-pixel-wide pattern.

The final exported pattern must:

  • be 48 pixels wide;
  • have a height between 1 and 1000 pixels;
  • be saved as an RGB PNG image;
  • contain exactly three distinct RGB colours.

The three colours can be selected directly from the editor palette.

2. Create the Pattern

Create the pattern using the Pattern Editor.

Choose one of the available editing modes:

  • Single Pattern to draw the complete 48-pixel-wide pattern directly;
  • Repeated Pattern to create an 8-pixel-wide module that is automatically repeated 6 times horizontally.

When using Repeated Pattern, the vertical structure can be created in two ways:

  • Repeat vertically: the same module is repeated a selected number of times;
  • Different modules: multiple 8-pixel-wide modules can be created, duplicated, reordered and assigned different heights.

The final preview always represents the actual 48 × H pixel pattern that will be exported.

Before saving, the editor checks that all three selected colours are actually used in the final pattern. The PNG cannot be saved unless it contains exactly three distinct colours.

When the pattern is saved, the editor also shows the colour-to-command interpretation used by the machine:

  • C1 / Servo 1
  • C2 / Servo 2
  • C3 / Servo 3

The mapping is determined by the order in which the three colours first appear in the final 48-pixel-wide pattern, reading the image from the first row onwards.

The editor can also:

  • open an existing compatible 48-pixel-wide, three-colour PNG;
  • import a PNG, JPEG, BMP or WebP image and automatically resize it to 48 pixels wide and reduce it to three colours.

Opened or imported images are loaded as a Single Pattern.

3. Copy the PNG to the USB Drive

After saving the pattern, copy the exported .png file directly into the root folder of the USB flash drive.

Example:

USB drive
├── flowers_pattern.png
├── stars_pattern.png
└── hearts_pattern.png

The files must not be placed inside subfolders.

When the copy is complete, safely eject the USB drive from the computer.

4. Raspberry Pi Software Setup

This setup must be performed on the Raspberry Pi inside the machine.

It is required only the first time the system is configured.

4.1 Install the Required System Packages

Open a terminal on the Raspberry Pi and install the required packages:

sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y python3-venv python3-pip

4.2 Create the Python Virtual Environment

Create a dedicated virtual environment:

mkdir -p /home/aless/venvs
python3 -m venv /home/aless/venvs/uncinetto

Activate it:

source /home/aless/venvs/uncinetto/bin/activate

Upgrade pip:

pip install --upgrade pip

4.3 Install the Required Python Libraries

Install the Python libraries used by the Raspberry Pi interface:

pip install pillow pyserial gfxhat

The libraries are used for:

Library Purpose
pillow Opening and validating PNG images
pyserial USB serial communication between Raspberry Pi and ESP32
gfxhat Managing the GFX HAT display and buttons

4.4 Enable Raspberry Pi Interfaces

The GFX HAT requires the Raspberry Pi hardware interfaces.

Open the configuration menu:

sudo raspi-config

Enable:

Interface Options → I2C → Enable
Interface Options → SPI → Enable

Then reboot the Raspberry Pi:

sudo reboot

4.5 Give Serial Permission to the User

To allow the Raspberry Pi user to access the ESP32 through USB serial, add the user to the dialout group:

sudo usermod -aG dialout $USER

Then reboot:

sudo reboot

5. Insert the USB Drive into the Machine

After creating the PNG on the user computer, insert the USB flash drive into the machine.

The Raspberry Pi inside the machine will read the PNG files from the USB drive.

6. Mount the USB Drive on the Raspberry Pi

Check the device name assigned to the USB drive:

lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,FSTYPE,LABEL,MOUNTPOINTS

In the current prototype, the USB drive is usually detected as:

/dev/sda1

Create the mount folder if it does not already exist:

sudo mkdir -p /mnt/pattern_usb

Mount the USB drive:

sudo mount /dev/sda1 /mnt/pattern_usb

Check that the PNG files are visible:

ls /mnt/pattern_usb

If the USB drive has a different device name, replace /dev/sda1 with the correct one.

7. Prepare the Hardware

Before starting a real test, verify that:

  • the Raspberry Pi is powered;
  • the GFX HAT display is connected to the Raspberry Pi;
  • the ESP32 is connected to the Raspberry Pi through its USB cable;
  • the three servomotors and the stepper are supplied by the external power supply;
  • all the GND are connected;
  • the microswitch is connected to the ESP32.

See Wiring and Power Supply for the complete connections.

8. Find the ESP32 Serial Port

Check which serial port is assigned to the ESP32:

ls /dev/ttyUSB*

or:

ls /dev/ttyACM*

In the current prototype, the ESP32 is usually available as:

/dev/ttyUSB0

If the ESP32 appears with a different name, use that port when running the application.

9. Start the Raspberry Pi Application

Activate the virtual environment:

source /home/aless/venvs/uncinetto/bin/activate

Run the integrated interface:

python3 /home/aless/raspberry.py --usb-dir /mnt/pattern_usb --port /dev/ttyUSB0

If the ESP32 is detected as /dev/ttyACM0, use:

python3 /home/aless/raspberry.py --usb-dir /mnt/pattern_usb --port /dev/ttyACM0

The command starts the Raspberry Pi interface, reads the PNG files from the USB drive and opens the serial communication with the ESP32.

10. Select the PNG from the Display

The display shows the files available on the USB drive:

SELEZIONA PNG
> flowers_pattern.png
  stars_pattern.png
  hearts_pattern.png
^v SPOSTA  OK SEL  + REF

Use:

Button Action
UP / DOWN Browse PNG files
SELECT Confirm the selected pattern
PLUS Refresh the file list

11. Insert the Yarns

After file selection, the display shows:

PATTERN SELEZIONATO
flowers_pattern.png

INSERIRE
I FILATI

+ AVVIA    < MENU

Place the three yarns consistently with the colour-to-servo mapping generated by the Raspberry Pi.

12. Start Production

Press PLUS (AVVIA).

The Raspberry Pi:

  1. validates the PNG file;
  2. checks that the image is 48 pixels wide;
  3. checks that the image contains exactly three RGB colours;
  4. opens the USB serial communication with the ESP32;
  5. sends the command corresponding to the first pixel.

13. Monitor the Process

While the system is running, the display shows:

flowers_pattern.png
IN LAVORAZIONE

[ progress bar ]

36%   18/50
- STOP

Every press of the synchronization microswitch causes the ESP32 to send a “NEXT” to the Raspberry Pi.

The Raspberry Pi then:

  1. moves to the following pixel;
  2. updates the percentage on the display;
  3. sends the next colour-selection command to the ESP32.

14. Pause and Resume

During processing:

Button Action
MINUS Pause the process and move all servo arms to DOWN
PLUS Resume from the preserved pixel
BACK Return to the file-selection menu from the stopped screen

When the process is paused, the current pixel index is preserved. When the user resumes the process, the system continues from the same position.

15. Completion

At the end of the pattern, all servos are moved to their inactive position and the display shows:

LAVORO
COMPLETATO

[ 100% ]

OK / < MENU

The user can then return to the menu and select another PNG file.

16. Unmount the USB Drive

Before removing the USB flash drive from the machine, unmount it safely:

sudo umount /mnt/pattern_usb

The USB drive can then be physically removed from the Raspberry Pi.

Current Limitation

The current stop/resume implementation acts on the three colour-selection servomotors.

Control of an additional main stepper drive is planned but is not part of the tested actuation firmware yet.

Common Commands

Operation Command
Run Pattern Editor on the user computer python3 pattern_editor.py
Activate Raspberry Pi virtual environment source /home/aless/venvs/uncinetto/bin/activate
Check USB drive name lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,FSTYPE,LABEL,MOUNTPOINTS
Mount USB drive on Raspberry Pi sudo mount /dev/sda1 /mnt/pattern_usb
Check ESP32 serial port ls /dev/ttyUSB*
Run machine interface python3 /home/aless/raspberry.py --usb-dir /mnt/pattern_usb --port /dev/ttyUSB0
Unmount USB drive sudo umount /mnt/pattern_usb
